questions.stem_markdown: A father in a Sydney paediatric clinic says, "My daughter is 17, so either she can always consent for herself or she cannot. Which is it?" What is the **best explanation** based on the notes?

options.text: Anyone under 18 can never consent to medical treatment for themselves
Once a young person turns 16, age alone is enough to decide competence
Capacity depends on factors such as maturity, understanding, and ability to weigh risks, benefits, and longer-term impacts, rather than age alone
A parent’s agreement automatically makes a minor competent to consent
School performance is the main determinant of legal competence

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes describe the **mature minor (Gillick competency)** as someone under 18 who is competent to consent, with competence assessed using factors such as maturity, intelligence, experience, understanding, ability to manage influences on decision-making, ability to weigh risks and benefits and longer-term impacts, and the seriousness of the treatment. Age alone is not the only determinant.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes state that some minors can be competent to consent as mature minors.
why_others_wrong.B: The source material does not treat age 16 alone as sufficient to establish competence.
why_others_wrong.D: Parental agreement is not listed as the determinant of a minor’s competence in the notes.
why_others_wrong.E: School performance is not the note-based test for consent capacity.

key_takeaways: Gillick competence is a capacity-based assessment, not a birthday threshold alone.
The notes emphasise understanding, maturity, and ability to weigh consequences.
Clinical explanation to families should focus on capacity rather than age alone.

questions.stem_markdown: Which adolescent most clearly fits the note-based description of a **mature minor** who may be competent to consent to medical treatment?

options.text: A 15-year-old who repeats a parent’s view but cannot explain the treatment risks or longer-term effects
A 14-year-old who knows the treatment name but cannot weigh alternatives or outside influences on the decision
A 16-year-old who explains the condition, the treatment options, the major risks and longer-term impacts, and can describe the decision in their own words despite family pressure
A 17-year-old who says age alone means doctors must accept any decision they make
A 13-year-old who bases the decision mainly on what a friend said happened to them

questions.explanation_markdown: The strongest fit is the young person who demonstrates the note-based markers of competence: **understanding**, ability to **weigh risks and benefits and longer-term impacts**, and ability to **manage influences on decision-making**. Those features are listed in the Louisa notes under mature minor (Gillick competency).

why_others_wrong.A: Repeating someone else’s view without understanding the risks and longer-term effects does not match the criteria in the notes.
why_others_wrong.B: Knowing a label without weighing alternatives or outside influences is weaker than the note-based standard.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes do not support age alone as enough to establish competence.
why_others_wrong.E: Basing the decision mainly on a friend’s experience does not show the maturity and independent reasoning described in the source material.

key_takeaways: Capacity is demonstrated through reasoning, not just confidence.
Ability to weigh longer-term impacts is specifically listed in the notes.
Managing outside influences is part of the mature minor assessment.

questions.stem_markdown: A 16-year-old can explain part of a proposed non-urgent treatment but struggles to weigh longer-term consequences. Which consent approach best matches the **intermediate understanding** row in the notes?

options.text: Consent from a parent or guardian must always be obtained, and the young person’s consent is not relevant
Consent from the young person may be sufficient, but consent from a parent or guardian should also be obtained unless the young person objects
Consent of the young person is always sufficient, even if understanding is incomplete
No consent is needed because a 16-year-old is presumed an adult for medical decisions
A court order is required for all treatment decisions at this level of understanding

questions.explanation_markdown: The table in the notes states that with **intermediate understanding**, consent from the young person **may be sufficient**, but consent of a parent or guardian **should also be obtained unless the young person objects**. This is more nuanced than either parent-only or adolescent-only approaches.

why_others_wrong.A: That is the recommendation for an immature and insufficient level of understanding, not the intermediate row.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes do not say that adolescent consent is always enough at this intermediate level.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes state that adults are 18 years and over, not 16 years and over.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes do not require a court order for all treatment decisions in this situation.

key_takeaways: The notes separate immature, intermediate, and mature understanding.
Intermediate understanding often still involves seeking parental consent as well.
Consent recommendations are graduated rather than all-or-none.

questions.stem_markdown: A 13-year-old arrives in the Emergency Department with a life-threatening condition and no parent can be contacted. According to the notes, what is the **best next step**?

options.text: Wait until a parent or guardian is reached before giving treatment
Proceed with emergency or life-saving treatment without the consent of the minor or parents
Treat only if two consultants independently agree
Do not treat unless the child is already assessed as Gillick competent
Transfer first for court authorisation

questions.explanation_markdown: The NSW consent points in the notes state that medical practitioners can carry out **emergency or life-saving treatment without the consent** of the minor or their parents. In an emergency, the immediate priority is treatment rather than delaying for formal consent.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes do not support delaying life-saving treatment while waiting for parental contact.
why_others_wrong.C: Two-consultant agreement is not the requirement stated in the source material.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes specifically allow emergency treatment without waiting for a mature minor assessment.
why_others_wrong.E: The court-order pathway is not the first step for an immediate life-saving emergency.

key_takeaways: Emergency treatment can proceed without prior consent in the situations described in the notes.
Delaying life-saving treatment for formal consent is not the note-based approach.
Emergency and non-urgent consent problems are handled differently.

questions.stem_markdown: A minor is scheduled for heart surgery, and the parents object in advance to a blood transfusion that may be needed during the operation. According to the notes, what additional step **may be required**?

options.text: Proceed as though parental refusal automatically settles the issue
Cancel the surgery until the child turns 18
Obtain a court order for further advice
Ask the anaesthetist to decide alone on the day
Treat the issue as irrelevant unless a complication actually occurs

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes state that if parents object to a **potentially foreseen emergency treatment**, such as a blood transfusion in a minor requiring heart surgery, it **might be necessary to obtain a court order for further advice**.

why_others_wrong.A: The source material does not say parental refusal automatically settles this type of case.
why_others_wrong.B: The notes do not suggest waiting until adulthood as the default response.
why_others_wrong.D: The note-based pathway mentions possible court involvement, not leaving the matter to a single clinician on the day.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes specifically use a foreseen emergency example, so the issue should not simply be ignored in advance.

key_takeaways: Foreseen emergency treatment can require planning before the emergency happens.
Parental refusal does not always end the consent pathway.
The notes specifically mention possible court advice for this type of scenario.

questions.stem_markdown: A 16-year-old with decision-making capacity refuses a recommended treatment. The parent asks whether that refusal always ends the matter. What is the **best response** based on the notes?

options.text: Yes, because any minor with capacity has an absolute right to refuse treatment
No, because a court can override a minor’s refusal to avoid serious consequences for the minor
No, because parents automatically decide whenever a minor refuses treatment
Yes, unless the treating team strongly disagrees
No, because every refusal by a minor must be reported to police

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes state that **a minor with capacity may refuse treatment**, but **a court can override this decision to avoid serious consequences for the minor**. This makes the refusal clinically important, but not always final in serious situations.

why_others_wrong.A: The source material specifically says a court can override the refusal in serious cases.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes do not say that parental wishes automatically replace the minor’s refusal in every situation.
why_others_wrong.D: Team disagreement alone is not the standard given in the notes.
why_others_wrong.E: Police reporting is not the note-based response to every refusal.

key_takeaways: A capable minor’s refusal still matters and should be taken seriously.
The notes allow for court override where serious consequences are at stake.
Counselling families requires explaining both respect for capacity and the limits of refusal in serious cases.

questions.stem_markdown: A parent refuses a recommended treatment for a younger child, and the team becomes concerned that the refusal could place the child at **risk of significant harm**. Which additional step does the notes say **may need to be considered**?

options.text: A Mandatory Report
Discharge from follow-up because the parent has made a final decision
Waiting until the child becomes a legal adult
Ignoring the refusal if one parent remains calm
Asking a sibling to consent instead

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes state that if a minor is **at risk of significant harm due to a parent’s refusal to consent**, clinicians may consider a **Mandatory Report**. This recognises that some consent conflicts move beyond disagreement into child-protection concern.

why_others_wrong.B: The notes do not support simply ending follow-up when harm risk is present.
why_others_wrong.C: Waiting until adulthood is not a safe or note-based response to possible significant harm.
why_others_wrong.D: Calm presentation by a parent does not remove the concern described in the source material.
why_others_wrong.E: A sibling is not the substitute decision-maker described in the notes.

key_takeaways: Parental refusal can become a child-protection issue if significant harm is likely.
The notes explicitly mention considering a Mandatory Report in that situation.
Consent conflict and safety concerns should be separated from routine family disagreement.

questions.stem_markdown: A 15-year-old and both parents disagree about a recommended treatment plan. According to the notes, what is the **best next step before considering a court order**?

options.text: Attempt to reach agreement by counselling and repeat discussion with the family
Proceed immediately on the parent’s preference only
Proceed immediately on the adolescent’s preference only
Stop discussing the plan and arrange no further follow-up
Delay any further action until the conflict settles on its own

questions.explanation_markdown: In the notes, one of the listed steps when there is refusal or conflict is to **attempt to reach agreement by counselling and repeat discussion with the family**. Court involvement is described as a **last resort**, not the first response once disagreement appears.

why_others_wrong.B: The notes do not say that the parent’s view automatically ends the dispute in all cases.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes do not present this as the automatic response to every conflict either.
why_others_wrong.D: Stopping follow-up is not part of the recommended approach in the source material.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes emphasise active management of conflict rather than passive delay.

key_takeaways: Counselling and repeat discussion are part of the conflict-resolution pathway in the notes.
Court orders are described as a last-resort measure.
Applied consent questions often focus on the next practical step, not just the legal label.

questions.stem_markdown: A 15-year-old is being considered for a treatment that is expected to cause **permanent infertility**. Which statement best matches the consent pathway in the notes?

Permanent infertility is specifically listed as a trigger for that pathway.
Neither parental consent nor mature minor consent is sufficient for this category in those under 16.

questions.stem_markdown: A 14-year-old wants more private control over Medicare access before attending clinic without a parent. Which advice is **most accurate** based on the notes?

At 14, only the adolescent can access online Medicare claims history, and a young person can have their own Medicare card from age 15

why_others_wrong.A: This contradicts both of the age thresholds stated in the notes.

why_others_wrong.D: The source material gives a threshold of 14 for online claims access by the adolescent.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes clearly describe specific Medicare changes during adolescence.

key_takeaways: The notes give specific Medicare age thresholds for adolescents.
Online Medicare claims history access changes at age 14.
A young person can have their own Medicare card from age 15.
